### Correlation Between Serum Lactate and Serum Citrate Levels

Serum lactate levels showed positive correlations with citrate levels at baseline, 6, 12, 24, 36, 48, and 72 hours after initiation of RCA-CRRT (r = 0.409, 0.436, 0.397, 0.390, 0.369, 0.351, and 0.433, respectively; P < 0.05, for all) (Supplementary Figure S2).

## Discussion

Our cohort is the largest prospective cohort to date with simultaneous measurements of serum citrate and lactate levels at standardized, prespecified time points. Here, we showed that serum lactate levels correlated positively with serum citrate levels throughout the RCA-CRRT sessions and were significantly higher in patients who developed CA than in those who did not. Notably, lactate levels at 6 and 12 hours showed excellent predictive capabilities for CA development, with close to 100% NPV. This highlights the great promise of serum lactate level in predicting CA during RCA-CRRT, because it is a commonly measured parameter and widely available even as a point-of-care test in the intensive care unit setting.

Although direct measurement of serum citrate levels showed excellent performance in diagnosing or predicting CA in patients receiving RCA-CRRT,3 the widespread application of direct citrate measurement is limited by availability of readily available assays, requirement for human resource, and long turn-around time. In contrast, lactate assays are available in most centers, require relatively less technical expertise, could be performed at the point-of-care, and are lower in costs. Here, we provided evidence on the correlations between serum lactate and citrate levels at various time points after initiation of RCA-CRRT. The time points at which serum lactate levels predict CA best, however, remain contested. One retrospective study suggested that serum lactate level at 18 hours post–RCA-CRRT showed the best AUROC compared with serum lactate level at baseline, 6, and 12 hours.4 Indeed, metabolism of both citrate and lactate requires oxygen.4 Gluconeogenesis from lactate and conversion of lactate to glucose both require adenosine triphosphate. Meanwhile, citrate is metabolized in the Krebs cycle via isocitrate dehydrogenase with hydrogen being transferred to nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide hydrogen . The regeneration of coenzyme nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide hydrogen to nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide+ is an oxygen dependent process. Although it is intuitive that later serum lactate levels better reflect the most recent physiological state of patients and hence better predict CA development, the choice of time points should consider both the precision for predicting CA development and room to alter the regimen to prevent CA. In this context, 6- and 12-hour serum lactate levels appear to be clinically useful time points, with good accuracy in predicting CA developing while allowing sufficient time to react.

The cut-off levels of 2.75 mmol/l and 2.95 mmol/l at 6 and 12 hours respectively, were shown to have very high predictive capabilities (AUROCs of 0.91 and 0.93, with high NPV of 1.00 and 0.99, respectively) and could effectively rule out CA in patients with serum lactate levels below this threshold. This is complementary to T:I Ca ratio, the most commonly employed surrogate for serum citrate levels, which was shown to offer mediocre sensitivity and specificity in in vitro and ex vivo studies of citrate pharmacokinetics.5,6 Another significant advantage of serum lactate over T:I Ca ratio is that it is not affected by confounding factors such as albumin level and pH.7,8 However, one should be mindful that we should not rely solely on a cut-off value but need to consider other parameters such as lactate kinetics, calcium ratio, or hypocalcemia requiring more calcium replacement to make circuit adjustment.

Limitations of this study include its observational nature, inclusion of only a derivation cohort without a separate validation cohort, and a relatively small number of patients who developed CA. In this study, clinicians had discretions to modify RCA-CRRT regimens in patients with established or impending CA and hence might influence our conclusions. Furthermore, lactate kinetics in critically ill patients showed slower normalization rates and altered metabolisms and thus may affect clinical applicability to predict CA. Notwithstanding, our results were generated from follow-up analysis of a multicenter prospective cohort with very few missing data. The findings highlight the promising role of serum lactate level in the algorithm of risk assessment and monitoring for CA during RCA-CRRT, and the cut-offs identified at various time points could be readily applied clinically. Future studies could be directed toward validating the result of the study in a bigger cohort with more diverse patient characteristics.

## Conclusion

Serum lactate levels at various time points were higher in patients receiving RCA-CRRT with CA, and showed significant correlations with blood citrate levels. Specifically, 6- and 12-hour lactate levels showed good performance for predicting development of CA.
